title: Specs Move to the Top Level
body: Your spec paths have a new root. The specs folder moved from `.opencode/specs/` to a physical top-level `specs/` directory, so canonical spec paths are now `specs/...`. **This is a breaking change**, but the old location still resolves through a compatibility symlink left in place, so anything still pointing at `.opencode/specs` keeps working while you catch up.

title: Reindexing Stops Rewriting Your Edits
body: A force reindex could write its own auto-fixes — including destructive content trimming — back into your tracked source documents, which is the last thing a "fix it up" operation should do. Write-back is now gated on where the indexing originated, so an automated pass can't reach into a document a human authored. The same gap was closed in the daemon's startup scan and file watcher, and the fix goes live once you restart the daemon.

title: Smaller Templates, Same Output
body:
The spec, plan, tasks, and implementation-summary templates were consolidated into one shared core with level-gated addenda, dropping the source from 2,931 to 1,314 lines without changing a single rendered byte. The research template now shrinks by level too, so a Level 1 spec gets a 175-line research doc instead of a 944-line one. You see smaller, level-appropriate templates; what they produce is identical.

The rest of the area is research charters still in planning, release-readiness audits, and a long pass normalizing archived packets to the current template set — real housekeeping, but nothing that changes how you use the system.

---

section: The Deep Loops, Unified and Extended
title: One Skill, Hub and Backend Together
body: The five-mode hub and the runtime it ran on are now a single skill, `system-deep-loop`. What had been two packages — the workflow hub and the backend runtime it sat over — merged into one, with every downstream reference (commands, agents, READMEs, hooks, advisor routing) repointed at the new home. The five modes you already use — research, review, council, context, improvement — behave exactly as before, and the deep router agent is now simply named `deep-loop`. What changed is the address: the `deep-loop-workflows` and `deep-loop-runtime` skill identities no longer exist, so anything you script that still names one of them now points at a signpost that isn't there.

section: The Deep Loops, Unified and Extended
title: A Conformance-Audit Mode
body:
A new `deep-alignment` mode joins the loop family. Hand it artifacts — docs, code, designs, git history — and it audits them against the named parent-skill authority they're supposed to follow, reusing the deep-review runtime engine so it stays consistent with the loops you already know. Working adapters already cover sk-doc, sk-git, sk-design (static and live-render), and sk-code. The mode is usable today; the packet's overall closeout is still in progress.

---

title: One Hub for the External CLIs
body: The six CLI-orchestrator skills now live under one canonical `cli-external-orchestration` hub, the same parent-over-modes shape the doc and prompt skills already use: the hub holds no logic of its own and routes to a mode per executor. The change is invisible where it counts — the concrete executor names like `cli-opencode` keep working — but two of them stop being independently routable top-level identities, so anything that pointed at `cli-opencode` or `cli-claude-code` as standalone skills now resolves through the hub instead.

title: Executors That Only Run When Installed
body: Codex and Devin are back, and Cursor and Pi are new. All four join as deep-loop executors — the peer AI tools the framework can hand work to — and every one is gated fail-closed on its own binary being present (a check like `command -v codex`, `cursor-agent`, `devin`, or `pi`). A missing tool simply never shows up as routable or dispatchable, rather than failing partway through a run. This is also a reversal of an earlier quiet removal: Codex and Devin had been deprecated and stripped out, then brought back this same way, so the roster you can actually use now matches what's really installed on your machine.

title: Surfaces Retired
body:
The Gemini and Copilot bridges are gone for good, removed end-to-end — skill, routing, runtime detection, and model references — after the Copilot price hike and the Gemini cleanup made them no longer worth maintaining. Copilot-shaped prompts now route to Claude Code instead. If you were still calling `cli-gemini` or `cli-copilot`, those are gone; only the external binaries sitting in your home directory are left untouched. One more thing arrived quietly, off by default: a portable plain-English projection layer in `sk-communication` that rewrites terse CLI output while keeping the original bytes intact, held out of routing until a human study clears it.

---

title: One Hub, Many Packets
body: The six-mode `sk-doc` monolith became a workflow-only parent hub that routes to self-contained `create-*` packets, the same two-axis shape `sk-code` and `sk-design` already use. A few things you type changed. Four `/create` commands were renamed to match their packet (`sk-skill` → `skill`, `folder_readme` → `readme`, and so on), the `doc-quality` packet is now `create-quality-control` with `/doc:quality` kept as an alias, and the documentation agent you call `@create` is now `@markdown`. The `/create:*` command family itself is untouched.

title: Three New Ways to Author
body: Three brand-new surfaces joined the terminal. `sk-create-diagram` turns out self-contained HTML/SVG diagrams across 27 types, imports and exports draw.io and Mermaid, and is reachable through the new `/create:diagram` command. A local-first diff engine compares a before and after document without git and produces a self-contained HTML report, so you can review an edit even when the file lives outside version control. And `sk-communication` routes agent output through a projection layer that gives you plain English while leaving the canonical bytes unchanged.

title: Kebab-Case Is Now the One Name
body: The repo settled on kebab-case as its single filesystem-naming form, retiring the older underscore convention. In-scope folders, files and scripts across the repo are renamed, a guard refuses new snake_case names, and a reviewable rename-and-reference toolchain keeps the migration honest. If you had a script or path pinned to an old underscore name, it may need updating.

title: Benchmarks, One Way
body:
Benchmark authoring now has a single home in `create-benchmark`, and every run lands in one dated folder grammar under `benchmark/reports/`. Two things to know: benchmark result paths moved to the new grammar, and `run-skill-benchmark.cjs` now exits with code 3 on structural or registry blocks instead of 0, so a blocked benchmark can no longer read as a passing one.

---

title: A Style Library You Own
body: You now have a design reference library that lives on your own machine instead of behind someone else's network call. All 1,290 Refero styles — each carrying four tabs — were pulled into a local token library (about 129 MB across 7,744 files), after a 50-style pilot came back clean. Around it sits a retrieval substrate that picks a style by eligibility first, and behind that a persistent style database built on SQLite with full-text search and vector lookup, so the corpus the modes study is the one you query. The payoff is speed: generating against the full 1,290-style corpus runs about 21x faster than the old path, with the legacy default kept until you flip it yourself.

title: Interface Creation Commands
body: Creating an interface is now a scripted conversation rather than an ad-hoc back-and-forth. A shared nine-stage contract under `/interface:*` walks you through the stages the same way every time, so a run is reproducible and gateable from the terminal. In the same pass, the ten command workflow files were brought onto the standard command vocabulary; the commands' runtime behavior is unchanged.

title: A Claude-Style Hub
body: Under the hood, the design hub was refactored to behave more like Claude Design while keeping OpenCode's native routing and its single advisor identity. It gained a manager-style shell and a private layer of fourteen procedure cards, with each mode pointing at its own procedures. For you, nothing about how you call it changed — the modes kept their authority and routing, and the md-generator's boundary stayed put. The work closed on a conditional parity verdict, with the live and browser scenarios left for you to confirm.

title: Open Design Transport Removed
body:
One transport leaves this release. The Open Design MCP transport is deprecated and removed end to end: its mode tree, server entry, hub references, agent and command links, and live-render adapters are all gone. If you still point at it, drop the `open_design` server from your `.utcp_config.json` and stop referencing `design-generation-patterns.md`; Figma and the terminal remain your design transports.

---

title: One Hub, Two Axes
body: The flat skill became a parent hub. It now routes on two axes at once: workflow modes (implement, quality, debug, verify and review) and read-only surface packets (webflow, opencode and animation), so the guidance you get is scoped to both what you're doing and the stack you're doing it to. All 128 relocated files were repointed — including a pre-commit hygiene gate that had been silently skipped — and a deterministic router benchmark rose from 44 to 71. This is the one place in the release with a hard breaking change: the routing contract and every skill path moved under the mode and surface packets, so anything that still points at the old flat paths must be updated.

title: Review, First Class
body: The review skill stops being a bolt-on. `sk-code-review` was renamed and rebuilt as a stack-agnostic review baseline, then folded into the hub as a mode. It now works on a baseline-plus-overlay precedence model: a shared baseline of findings-first review rules, with stack-specific guidance layered on top rather than each stack carrying its own copy. It is wired across the review runtime, orchestrators, Codex agents and the advisor, so the same standard shows up everywhere you ask for one. One caveat survives: the doc validators still reject the skill's hyphenated name.

title: Rust Joins the Code
body: Rust is now a first-class citizen on the opencode surface. The standard docs are in place, `.rs` files and Cargo projects are detected, and routing covers both child and parent-union layouts, so a Rust change surfaces the Rust guidance instead of the generic fallback. Six registration touchpoints were wired and verified with a fail-closed router replay. For everyone else, the same pass split 33 oversized reference documents into 104 topic-cohesive parts, so the files you load are shorter and closer to the point.

title: Deprecated Skills Retired
body:
The old `sk-code-web` and `sk-code-full-stack` skills are gone. Their cross-references were pruned across the tree and the umbrella's placeholder pointers were neutralized, but the real cost is worth naming: by decision, roughly three dozen files of canonical React, Node, Go and Swift guidance left the tree with them. If you relied on those pages, they are no longer there to fall back to.

---

title: Every Commit Reaches Your IDE
body: Your editor now reflects work you never touched in it. A trunk-following pipeline autosyncs each commit from a wrapper-launched Claude, Codex, or OpenCode session onto one shared live branch, behind three checks (an environment flag, a linked worktree, and installed hooks), and a fast-forward follower keeps your IDE checkout current. So when a background session lands work, it is already sitting there when you look.

title: Remote Push Is Curated By Default
body: Pushing no longer happens silently. Only `main`, `skilled/v*` releases, and names you have added to an allowlist file go up without asking; every other push needs a fresh, in-the-moment go-ahead. The rule is enforced twice — as a rule agents must follow, and as a `pre-push` hook that also catches human pushes. If you have an in-flight branch like `origin/skilled/0064-*`, expect it to hit this gate on its next push.

title: A Fail-Open Guard Against Mass Deletion
body: A single stale `git add -A` once erased 902 files, and a runaway agent can do the same. That path now has a tripwire: a guard blocks any commit or push that removes more than a threshold (default 100) of tracked files, unless you authorize the one operation with an explicit flag. It is live for commits now and ready for pushes, and it fails open when it cannot verify, so it never wedges you.

title: Owner-First Branch Names
body:
Branches now carry their owner. The grammar is `<skill>/{NNNN}-{slug}` (or `skilled/{NNNN}-{slug}`), and the number is allocated by a locked clone-wide counter, so two sessions cannot grab the same one. This is a breaking change: older `wt/`-style names no longer conform and new branches must follow the owner-first form, though the gate that checks them is deliberately tolerant of existing names and never blocks a `skilled/v*` release.

Also folded in: a command-time advisory surfaces the relevant git rule the moment a git command runs, the resource paths moved to hyphen-case as the first step of a repo-wide migration, and the GitKraken MCP was wired in for those who use it.

---

title: One Hub for Prompt Craft
body: `sk-prompt` is now the single home for prompt work, running two modes over one shared structure: `prompt-improve` for turning a rough prompt into a structured one, and `prompt-models` for the per-model profiles. The old `/prompt:improve` command was a 28KB monolith; it's now a thin router with its auto, confirm and presentation pieces split into their own files. The breaking change is one command name: `/prompt` is now `/prompt-improve`, and everything that lived in the standalone `sk-prompt-models` skill moved under `sk-prompt/prompt-models/`.

title: A Profile for Every Model
body: The per-model prompt-craft knowledge is now a real hub with nine conformed profiles, one per small model, and a `recommended_frameworks` field on all eight models so routing can suggest which of the eleven prompt frameworks fits the model you're calling. The five CLI skills each carry a single three-tier precedence rule for composing prompts instead of around 90 lines of duplicated quality cards. The knowledge sits in three layers — framework tables in `sk-prompt`, per-model profiles in the `prompt-models` mode, and lean delegating mirrors in the `cli-*` executors — so a model's profile lives in exactly one place.

title: The Names Settle
body:
The renames that started in earlier releases closed out here, and they're breaking wherever a reference crosses the boundary. The skill went `sk-improve-prompt` → `sk-prompt`, the models skill went `sk-prompt-small-model` → `sk-prompt-models`, and the agent went `@improve-prompt` → `@prompt-improver`. If anything still references `sk-prompt-small-model`, update it to `sk-prompt-models`; the advisor already resolves the new name at full confidence.

---

title: One Hub for the MCP Bridges
body: Every bridge now lives under a single `mcp-tooling` parent instead of standing alone, so the browser, ClickUp and design tools are one skill that reads which mode you want and routes to it. It is the sixth canon-clean parent in the framework — one of the hubs that meets the full documentation and routing standard — and it ships the feature catalogs, install front doors and worked examples the other parents already had. The router underneath it now does what its name promises: an intent that once replayed correctly six times out of thirteen now replays correctly all thirteen, backed by a hard gate that refuses to ship if any packet routes wrong.

title: Three Transports and a Browser Bridge
body: The hub's shelf grew this release. Two read-only design-reference transports joined it — `mcp-refero` searches styles, screens and flows, and `mcp-mobbin` does design research — and both defer to the design-judgment skill for taste, so they gather references rather than make decisions. `mcp-aside-devtools` adds a browser bridge, driving the agentic `aside` browser from its command line with a server fallback for when the CLI is not enough.

title: Your Vault at the Terminal
body: `mcp-obsidian` walks your notes vault out to the terminal. One mode covers three paths — a headless notes CLI, the official app-backed CLI, and a community MCP server — with a feature catalog and references for the plugins you are most likely to lean on. The work is honest about its rough edges: title search is broken headlessly so the mode uses content search instead, and the installed REST API exposes a different tool set than the documented server, a gap still awaiting reconciliation.

title: Figma Leaves the Tree
body:
This is the one change you may need to act on. The local `mcp-figma` developer skill is withdrawn, and Figma work now routes to a separate Figma agent that lives outside this repo. If you had scripts or habits pointing at the local skill, repoint them at the external agent.

---

title: Goals in Every Tool
body: Your session goal now means the same thing in every tool you open. The goal system that started in OpenCode ports to Devin, Cursor and Pi through a shared core and a common active-goal store, so a goal you set carries the same weight wherever you work. Honesty was part of the port: live capability probes recorded what each tool can actually do rather than what it claims, so Cursor is marked injection-only and Pi observes without verifying. On the way, goals stopped living as one global singleton — they are now stored per workspace, runtime and session, so two projects cannot see each other's goals. **Breaking:** a goal saved under the old global scheme no longer injects; it sits in a diagnostic-only state until you migrate or archive it explicitly.

title: Pi Chooses Its Own Path
body: When you hand Pi a subtask, it now hands it to its own subagents by default. Pi subagent dispatch defaults to native pi-subagents unless you explicitly name a `cli-*` mode, so a general request uses Pi's workers instead of quietly routing out to another model. **Breaking:** this is a changed default — name the `cli-*` mode when you want a specific executor.

title: Snappier Pi
body: Pi stopped stalling on the way to your message. The input hook that used to block every send on a chain of separate processes now runs its advisor in-process, so a repeat prompt resolves from the advisor's own five-minute cache in about a millisecond instead of a second and a half. A false "deleted skill" invalidation bug was fixed along the way, and only the ~1.3 second cold start on a brand-new prompt remains.

title: One Switch for the Hooks
body:
All twenty hook concerns now report to a single switch. A master flag, `MK_HOOKS_DISABLED`, turns the entire cross-runtime hook layer off at once, with a canonical flag for each of the twenty concerns beneath it and the old aliases kept working. If you want a personal default, put it in `hook-flags.env` — live environment values win, and a missing file fails open.

Beyond those, the Gate-3 spec question now stays quiet on read-only turns, and the hook reference docs moved into their owning trees — small things, no behavior change.

---

title: A Standalone Advisor with a Skill Graph
body: The advisor now routes with more than keyword matching. It grew a graph backbone — 21 per-skill metadata files recording how skills enhance, depend on, or conflict with one another — and a compiler that validates those edges, so the routing score now gets a boost from the relationships between skills rather than only the words in your prompt. In the same pass the advisor was extracted into its own standalone `system-skill-advisor` package with its own launcher, its database renamed, and every consumer cut over to it.

title: A Command-Line Front Door
body: You can now drive the advisor from the command line. The `mk_skill_advisor` server gained a manifest-backed, byte-identical 9-tool CLI fallback, hardened with scorer-parity, orphan-reaping, and a three-daemon spawn drill. One breaking change to know: warm-only CLI invocation is now mandatory on prompt paths, because the one-shot native bridge measured 824.8ms — too slow to sit on the path every session hits. The Python `skill_advisor.py` facade stays in place for backward compatibility.

title: A Faster, Safer Warm Path
body: The path that runs every session got faster and stricter. Warm-path matching now uses in-process caching with mtime invalidation and frontmatter-only parsing, plus a structural batch mode, so a warm answer lands in 0.61ms against 46.99ms for the cold subprocess path — roughly a 25x gap, now pinned by permanent regression and benchmark harnesses. On the safety side, uncertainty guarding stays on by default even when you pass `--threshold`, unless you explicitly ask for confidence-only.

title: Codex Starts the Advisor
body:
Codex sessions now launch the advisor under the Node 25 runtime (ABI 141) that matches the installed native SQLite module, so `mk_skill_advisor` initializes instead of aborting the whole MCP startup cascade. Memory and code mode keep their own independent runtime pins.

---

title: Terminal Proof Is Now the Law
body: The rule that a claim needs proof is no longer a separate protocol you opt into and keep in sync. It is now distributed across the authorities you already follow — the Four Laws, the Verification Standards, the Blast-Radius rules, a new Final-State Verification gate, Execution Behavior, and the Quick Reference — so it reads as one coherent instruction rather than a standalone lifecycle block. The per-turn reminder each session shows now carries a proof-over-appearance line through the existing governor chain, and the change shipped with the directive-expectation tests green.

title: Communication Quality §8
body:
Every runtime now finds its cross-runtime communication rules in one place. A new Communication Quality section spells out how answers should be written — one idea per sentence, a recommendation that has to earn itself, the request restated before diving in — rather than leaving those standards scattered or implicit. The deeper Codex voice spec was reconciled with four additive edits so the two documents agree, and only the genuinely new craft was lifted from the source; roughly seventy percent of it was already covered, and covered more thoroughly, elsewhere.

---
